lessons.title: Read for the gist
lessons.tip: The gist is the big idea of a text: what it is mostly about. Before you look for small facts, read the whole text once, quickly, and ask, “What is this about?” Do not stop for every new word.
sources: CEFR Companion Volume (reading and listening descriptors, A1-A2)
Plain-language reading practice conventions (gist, detail, scanning); texts written for this app

lessons.title: Find the detail
lessons.tip: A detail is one small fact: a name, a place, a time, a reason. Read the question first. Then read the text again and look for the words that answer it. Question words such as who, when and where tell you what kind of detail to find.
sources: CEFR Companion Volume (reading and listening descriptors, A1-A2)

lessons.title: Scan for facts
lessons.tip: To scan, move your eyes over the text and look for only one thing, such as a number, a name or a day. You do not read every word. Look for capital letters (names), digits (numbers) and special words like Monday.
sources: CEFR Companion Volume (reading and listening descriptors, A1-A2)

lessons.title: Listen for key words
lessons.tip: When you listen, you cannot go back, so listen for the key words: the important names, numbers, places and actions. Little words like “the” and “a” are quiet and quick. Ask yourself: who is speaking, what do they want, and when or where?
sources: CEFR Companion Volume (reading and listening descriptors, A1-A2)

lessons.title: Skim, then scan
lessons.tip: Skimming means reading fast to get the general idea: look at the title, the first sentence of each paragraph and the last line. Scanning means looking for one fact, such as a name, number or date, without reading every word. Skim first to know what the text is, then scan for the detail you need. Do not stop at every new word.
sources: British Council-EAQUALS Core Inventory for General English (topic order and level)
CEFR Companion Volume (reading and listening descriptors, A2-B1)

lessons.title: Paragraphs and topic sentences
lessons.tip: A paragraph usually has one main idea. The topic sentence states it, often at the start. The other sentences give details, examples or reasons. Read the first sentence of each paragraph to follow the text quickly. If you can say what each paragraph is about in a few words, you have understood the structure.

lessons.title: What does “it” mean?
lessons.tip: Writers avoid repeating words, so they use pronouns such as it, they, this and them. To understand a text, find what each pronoun points to. It usually refers to the nearest noun before it that fits. “The club is free. It meets monthly.” Here it means the club. If you are unsure, replace the pronoun with the noun and check that the sentence makes sense.
sources: British Council-EAQUALS Core Inventory for General English (topic order and level)
CEFR Companion Volume (reading and listening descriptors, A2-B1)

lessons.title: Follow a sequence
lessons.tip: Instructions and stories often use time words to show order: first, then, next, after that, finally. They help you picture what happens and in which order. When you read instructions, number the steps. If the order is not clear, look for words like before and after. “Before you serve it” means serving comes later than the earlier steps.
sources: British Council-EAQUALS Core Inventory for General English (topic order and level)
CEFR Companion Volume (reading and listening descriptors, A2-B1)

lessons.title: Numbers, times and prices
lessons.tip: In speech, numbers go quickly, and some sound alike: thirteen and thirty, fifteen and fifty. Listen for the stress: thirTEEN has stress on the end; THIRty on the start. Times can be said in different ways: “half past four,” “four thirty.” Prices: “twelve fifty” can mean 12.50. Write the numbers as digits while you listen.

lessons.tip: To follow spoken instructions, listen for action words: turn, press, open, wait. Listen for order words and for numbers. Repeat or write short notes: left 2nd street. lessons.title: Read between the lines
lessons.tip: A writer does not always say everything. An inference is a conclusion you reach from clues in the text plus what you already know. When a shop sign says “Back in ten minutes” but an hour has passed and letters are piling up, you can infer that the owner is away longer than planned. Check that your inference fits all the clues, and avoid going beyond them.
sources: British Council-EAQUALS Core Inventory for General English (topic order and level)

lessons.title: Purpose and tone
lessons.tip: Every text has a purpose: to inform, persuade, entertain or warn. Tone is the writer’s attitude: neutral, enthusiastic, critical, humorous. Look at the word choice. “A tragic mistake” is critical; “a few changes” is neutral. An ad wants you to act; a report wants you to understand. Asking “Why was this written?” helps you decide how far to trust it.

CEFR Companion Volume (reading and listening descriptors, B1-B2)

lessons.title: Follow an argument
lessons.tip: An argument has a claim, reasons and sometimes a counterclaim. To follow it, find the claim first: what does the writer want you to accept? Then find the reasons and the evidence. Words like because, since and therefore signal reasons. But, however and although signal a different view. A strong text answers the other side. Ask: do the reasons actually support the claim?

lessons.title: Summarize a text
lessons.tip: A summary gives the main points in your own words, much shorter than the original. Find the main idea, then the two or three key supports. Leave out examples, repetition and small details. Do not add your opinion. Use reporting phrases: “The writer argues that…” “According to the report…”. A good summary can be understood without reading the original.

CEFR Companion Volume (reading and listening descriptors, B1-B2)

lessons.title: Listen for attitude
lessons.tip: In speech, how something is said can change its meaning. Stress on a word shows what matters most: “I didn’t say HE took it” differs from “I didn’t SAY he took it.” Rising intonation at the end often shows a question or doubt; falling intonation shows a statement or certainty. A speaker who says “Oh, great” with a flat voice may not be happy at all. Listen for tone as well as words.
sources: British Council-EAQUALS Core Inventory for General English (topic order and level)
CEFR Companion Volume (reading and listening descriptors, B1-B2)

lessons.title: Compare two sources
lessons.tip: When two texts describe the same event, compare them. What facts do both include? What does only one include? Do their numbers match? Is one more detailed or more careful? lessons.title: Spot loaded words and bias
lessons.tip: Bias is a leaning toward one side. Loaded words carry feeling: “The council forced through a pointless lane” is more loaded than “The council approved a lane.” Look for one-sided evidence, missing voices and words like obviously and everyone knows. A biased text is not always false, but you should check its claims in a second source. Replace loaded words with neutral ones to see what the facts are.

CEFR Companion Volume (reading and listening descriptors, B1-B2)

lessons.title: Irony, understatement and implication
lessons.tip: Writers often mean more, less or the opposite of what they say. Irony says one thing while signaling another: praising a timetable and then advising everyone to allow an extra hour. Understatement plays down: “a slight delay” for a day of chaos. Implication leaves a conclusion unsaid. To read these, notice the gap between the words and the situation, and ask what the writer wants you to conclude. Context is your main clue.
sources: British Council-EAQUALS Core Inventory for General English (topic order and level)

lessons.title: Rhetorical moves in a text
lessons.tip: Persuasive texts use recognizable moves. A false dilemma presents two options as the only ones. Loaded contrast pits good against bad. Rhetorical questions imply an answer. Repetition builds emotion. Appeals to authority or fear stand in for evidence. Spotting them does not mean the argument is wrong; it means you should look at the evidence behind the style. Ask: what is being asked of me, and what support is given?

CEFR Companion Volume (reading and listening descriptors, C1-C2)

lessons.title: Evaluate evidence and methods
lessons.tip: When a text cites a study, ask how it was done. Who took part, and how were they chosen? How many? Was there a comparison group? Who paid for it, and could that affect the result? Does the conclusion go beyond the data? A claim of cause needs more than a correlation. Treat a single study with caution and look for replication. The question is not whether the study is perfect but how far the conclusion can be trusted.

CEFR Companion Volume (reading and listening descriptors, C1-C2)

lessons.title: Synthesize several sources
lessons.tip: Synthesis means building one view from several sources. Do not summarize each in turn. Group the sources by idea: where do they agree, disagree, or answer different questions? Weigh their quality: sample, method, date. Then state a position that accounts for all of them: “Surveys of managers suggest gains, but a controlled trial of call-center staff found losses, so the effect may depend on the type of work.” Attribute each point clearly.

lessons.title: Long talks and digressions
lessons.tip: In a long lecture or talk, speakers digress, return, qualify and repeat. Follow the main thread: listen for signposts (“to return to my main point,” “the second issue”), and for restatements (“in other words”). Separate main points from asides: “by the way” and “this reminds me” mark digressions. Keep a running outline, leave gaps for what you miss, and use the summary at the end to check it. Do not panic if you lose a detail: rejoin at the next signpost.
sources: British Council-EAQUALS Core Inventory for General English (topic order and level)
CEFR Companion Volume (reading and listening descriptors, C1-C2)

lessons.title: Fast, reduced and accented speech
lessons.tip: Natural speech is not careful speech. Words blend and reduce: “going to” becomes “gonna,” “want to” becomes “wanna,” “did you” sounds like “didja.” Function words are weak and quick; content words carry stress. Accents differ in vowels, consonants and rhythm, so a word may sound unlike the dictionary form. To train your ear, listen to the same speaker several times, use captions to check afterward, and focus on the stressed words first. Context often fills the gaps.
sources: British Council-EAQUALS Core Inventory for General English (topic order and level)
CEFR Companion Volume (reading and listening descriptors, C1-C2)

lessons.title: Follow a debate or interview
lessons.tip: In a debate or interview, speakers disagree, interrupt and talk across each other. Track who holds which position; note each speaker’s claim in a word or two. Listen for stance markers: “frankly,” “I’d argue that,” “to be fair.” Notice when a speaker concedes, deflects or changes the subject. Do not confuse a speaker repeating an opponent’s view (“You say that…”) with their own. After listening, summarize each position in one sentence.

CEFR Companion Volume (reading and listening descriptors, C1-C2)

lessons.title: Tone shifts and subtle register
lessons.tip: Skilled speakers and writers change tone within a single piece: formal to confiding, serious to playful, distant to personal. Notice the signals: sentence length, vocabulary, direct address (“you”), humor and contractions. A shift often marks something important: the move from policy language to a personal story signals a turning point. Ask what the shift does for the audience. Reading for tone is not only decoding words; it is hearing how the writer or speaker stands toward the topic and the reader.

CEFR Companion Volume (reading and listening descriptors, C1-C2)
